questions.prompt: An attack function adds ε·sign(w) to inputs of a +1-labelled example. What happens to the accuracy-under-attack curve?
options: It stays constant, since the perturbation is a fixed direction and size
It rises with ε because the sign is wrong: the attack should subtract, not add
It falls with ε as designed, since the perturbation grows with the budget
It oscillates randomly, because the sign of w changes with each example
questions.explanation: The worst case moves against the margin: x − t·ε·sign(w).
questions.skillLabel: Worst-case margin of a linear classifier

questions.prompt: |H|=100, δ=0.1, n=2000. What is the Hoeffding gap? (decimal, tolerance 0.0005)
How many samples guarantee a gap of at most 0.05 for |H|=10⁴ and δ=0.05? (integer, tolerance 2)
The Hoeffding bound for a deep network class is vacuous (larger than 1). What can you conclude about the network's test performance?
options: The network must generalize well, because the bound is only an upper limit
The test accuracy is exactly 50%, because the bound exceeds one
The network must overfit, since a vacuous bound means it memorises
Nothing directly: the bound is loose, so measure held-out performance
questions.explanation: A vacuous bound is an absence of a guarantee, not evidence of failure.

questions.prompt: Learning-curve points (n=1,000, loss 0.40) and (n=100,000, loss 0.10) on a pure power law. What loss does it predict at n=10⁷? (decimal, tolerance 0.003)
questions.explanation: Loss falls 4× per 100× data (α=0.301); another 100× gives 0.10/4=0.025.

questions.prompt: Compute C ≈ 6ND (in units of 10²¹ FLOPs) for N=2×10⁹ parameters and D=40×10⁹ tokens. (decimal, tolerance 0.01)
You fit loss ∝ n^−α to data that actually follow c + a·n^−α with c>0, using only small n. What is the typical result?
options: A flatter apparent slope and over-optimistic or inconsistent extrapolation
A steeper apparent slope, and over-pessimistic extrapolation to large n
An undefined exponent, because the log of c + a·n^−α cannot be taken
An exact fit, because a pure power law contains the floor as a special case
questions.explanation: The floor bends the log-log curve toward horizontal; the straight-line fit mixes both effects.

questions.prompt: Logistic regression with w=(2,−1,1), b=0, x=(1,1,3), label +1. Worst-case loss over ‖δ‖∞≤0.75 is ζ(ε‖w‖₁−m) with ζ(z)=ln(1+eᶻ). Compute it (decimal, tolerance 0.002).
questions.explanation: Margin m=2−1+3=4. ‖w‖₁=2+1+1=4, so ε‖w‖₁=0.75·4=3. Worst-case loss ζ(3−4)=ζ(−1)=ln(1+e^{−1})=0.3133. The clean loss ζ(−4)=0.0181 is much smaller, so the attack matters; a common mistake is to use ‖w‖₂ or to subtract ε‖w‖₁ from the loss instead of the margin.
questions.skillLabel: Worst-case loss of adversarially trained logistic regression

questions.prompt: For g(θ,δ)=θδ with δ∈[−ε,ε] and φ(θ)=max_δ g, you run the Danskin recipe at θ=0 using the maximiser δ=ε and step along −∇θ g. What happens?
options: φ decreases, because −∇θ g is always a descent direction of the max-function
φ is unchanged, because the gradient at a maximiser is zero when the maximiser is not unique
φ increases to ε²τ for step τε, because at a non-unique maximiser the directional derivative is ε|h| in every direction
φ becomes undefined, because the maximum does not exist on a compact interval
questions.explanation: φ(θ)=ε|θ|, so φ(0)=0 and the argmax at θ=0 is the whole interval. Danskin gives φ'(0;h)=sup_δ hδ=ε|h|>0 for every h≠0, so every step, including −ε·τ, raises φ (to τε²). The gradient at one maximiser (ε) describes only one side of the kink. The set-valued argmax is why the recipe needs a unique maximiser. The max exists because the interval is compact.
questions.skillLabel: Danskin's theorem and descent directions for min-max training

questions.prompt: In the parametric loss E+A/N^α+B/D^β with α=0.34, β=0.28 and the constraint 6ND=C, the compute budget is multiplied by 100. By what factor does the optimal N grow? (decimal, tolerance 0.1)
questions.explanation: N_opt ∝ C^a with a=β/(α+β)=0.28/0.62=0.4516. So the factor is 100^0.4516=10^0.9032=8.00. (Using the other exponent α/(α+β)=0.5484 would give 12.5, which is the growth of D.) Optimising N and D each by the square root (a=b=0.5) would give 10, which is the equal-scaling answer only when α=β.
questions.skillLabel: Compute-optimal allocation from a parametric loss
